This may actually be a bigger speedup than I initially thought.

The current method has a cost of ``(M+1)**2*(2*N+1)*(Mnodes+1)**2*(2*Nnodes+1)`` FLOPs
using an fft, assuming you need to do ``2*N+1`` matrix multplies each of size ``(M+1)**2*(Mnodes+1)**2`` to go from zernike to fourier for each n, followed by ``(M+1)**2*(Mnodes+1)**2`` each of length ``2*Nnodes+1`` (ie, taking the fft in the toroidal direction at each gridpoint on a poloidal cut), 
then the fft method would use ``(2*N+1)*(M+1)**2*(Mnodes+1)**2 + (Mnodes+1)**2*(2*Nnodes+1)*np.log(2*Nnodes+1)`` FLOPs

The speedup depends mostly on N and Nnodes, summarized below for different oversampling rates (Nnodes = N*oversample)
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/22567458/94390238-18b49080-0120-11eb-8756-95f206690328.png)

We could also look into doing a weighted least squares thing (effectively using a larger error ratio just for the perturbation stuff) or regularized as well by penalizing large changes in the low mode numbers

The checkpointing needs to be updated so that it saves the boundary and pressure inputs that were being solved at that iteration, according to the `bdry_ratio` and `pres_ratio` parameters.  For instance, if the equilibrium at the current iteration was computed with `pres_ratio = 0` then the data should be saved as a vacuum solution not whatever pressure profile was input.  It might also be good to note the value of `zeta_ratio` since anything other than unity isn't really a true equilibrium.

The issue was a bug in the boundary condition function.  This line: 
```
# ratio of non-axisymmetric boundary modes to use
ratio = jnp.clip(bdry_ratio+(bdryN == 0), 0, 1)
```
needed to be replaced with:
```
ratio = jnp.where(bdryN != 0, bdry_ratio, 1)
```
The performance might still be affected by the choice of `errr_ratio` weight.

There is now an option for symmetric nodes, which uses the `stell_sym` input parameter.  All it does is remove the nodes with: 
(zeta > 2pi/NFP)  and also  (zeta = 0 AND theta > pi)
This reduces the total number of nodes by almost half.  Convergence appears to be worse than expected after this change. 

The "proper" symmetric node setup is more nuanced.  The number of nodes (and pattern to use) should depend on the Zernike indexing (ANSI/Fringe).  Also, the f_beta equations should not be evaluated at theta=zeta=0, since those equations are trivially satisfied.  More work will be needed on this.  

If we were doing a true spectral collocation method, we would need to oversample by at least 1.5x in both M and N.  We probably need to test to see what gives us the best convergence, which may be problem dependent.

If we want to fit N Fourier coefficients we need to interpolate at at least N nodes.  However, when there is symmetry we also only need half of the boundary Fourier coefficients. Looked into this more and it's probably not worth it. Not having to evaluate the full jacobian is nice, but the operator is pretty poorly conditioned so the iterative methods take a while, and you also need to relinearize the whole thing at each new point in the optimization, so for the cases I tested its pretty slow. Scalar minimization with BFGS is a better option for high res cases.

Marking this as won't fix, but the idea of using iterative methods would still make sense to save memory for the 2nd order perturbations (there we only need hessian vector products, not the inverse so the condition number doesnt matter as much)

The DESC paper is still on my to-read stack, but is it fair to say tokamak calculations will generally converge faster than stellarator ones, due to axisymmetry making things easier?

Yes, axisymmetric inputs are generally easier to converge for two main reasons:
1. DESC currently assumes nested flux surfaces.  This is always true for tokamaks, but arbitrary stellarator solutions with nested flux surfaces are not guaranteed to exist.  
2. Stellarators require multiple toroidal Fourier modes to resolve the non-axisymmetric geometry, which increases the dimensionality of the problem.  

If you have any questions while reading the DESC paper, please reach out to me: [ddudt@princeton.edu](ddudt@princeton.edu).  Thank you for using the code and identifying issues!

Re: the first concern about super().init

For a class structure with multiple inheritances, Python will check the parents in the order they are listed.  In the following example, the Child constructor will call the constructor of Parent1: 
```
class Child(Parent1, Parent2):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
````
If `Parent1` does not have the desired method, then it will check `Parent2`.  Then it would check the parent of `Parent1`, then the parent of `Parent2`, etc.

So we just need to make sure that we list "primary" parents first, and other parents like `IOAble` afterwards. 

Reference: [https://stackoverflow.com/questions/3277367/how-does-pythons-super-work-with-multiple-inheritance](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/3277367/how-does-pythons-super-work-with-multiple-inheritance)

After a fair amount of testing, it seems like `ftol=1e-4` and `nfev=50` is pretty reasonable. Going for tighter tolerances and more iterations can get to lower error, but the rate of convergence slows down a lot so its usually better to go for fewer iterations per step and more resolution steps to get to higher resolution. This also helps to avoid overfitting the basis.

For perturbations, its usually best to start from a vacuum tokamak, then increase pressure, then perturb into a stellarator. The size of the perturbation steps depends somewhat on how "complicated" the perturbations are, but steps of 0.25 seems fairly conservative. For simple cases you can do that full perturbation in 1 step.

Along these lines, all of the compute methods of configuration use more derivatives than strictly needed. Rather than just setting derivs=1 or 2 we should only have the transforms compute the ones that are necessary

Hi, thanks for raising the issue!

For your first point on perturbing the flux surfaces, the slight difference you see between the documentation and your local execution is something I am able to reproduce as well, so I believe that is just a product of changes made to the code slightly changing the outcome of that particular perturbation. Thanks for letting us know, we can update the docs with a more recent run of that notebook.

When you use eq.perturb, we do not expect the force balance to be zero after the perturbation, so that is expected behavior. What is being done is we are expanding the equilibrium force balance equation f(x,c)=0 in a taylor series with respect to changes in x (the state vector of flux surface positions R,Z, represented in DESC as the coefficients of the Fourier-Zernike basis) and changes in c (the other parameters needed to solve a fixed-boundary equilibrium, so pressure, iota, boundary shape, etc). We then set f(x + dx, c + dc) = 0, and find the dx needed to satisfy this equation to the specified order for the given dc (which can be a change in pressure or change from 2D to 3D boundary). Since it is basically a taylor series approximation, the perturbed equilibrium is not expected to be in perfect force balance, but it is often a good initial guess for the final equilibrium solution ( as you can see looking at the perturbed DSHAPE equilibrium you have versus the final solved equilibrium).

As for the differences in the DSHAPE equilibrium, the input file and the equilibrium in the paper were solved assuming stellarator 
up-down symmetry (in input files this is the line that reads `sym = 1`), which can be set by adding `"sym": True`  to your input dictionary in your `high_beta_D.txt` file (this is set to False by default currently when a new `Equilibrium` object is created. If you do so, you can see that the resulting solution after perturbing and then solving is similar to the VMEC solution using the below code:

```python
from desc.vmec import VMECIO # needed to load VMEC .nc files
import netCDF4 # needed for VMECIO
vmec_file = 'examples/VMEC/wout_DSHAPE.nc' # path to the VMEC DSHAPE solution
VMECIO.plot_vmec_comparison(eq1,vmec_file)
```

You can see that the two solutions have identical flux surfaces, with only slight differences in the theta contours.

Dario covered most of it. In some cases, things will still be in equilibrium after a perturbation, but it obviously depends on the magnitude of the perturbation. The D shape example goes from beta=0 to beta=3% which is probably a bit too big to keep things in equilibrium but still should give reasonable flux surfaces by eye. I've found that in many cases stepping beta in increments of 1% produces reasonably well converged solutions with just the perturbation.

As for the symmetry issue, in theory you should get the same answer if you don't enforce symmetry explicitly (its just using more modes than necessary). We've done most of our testing with symmetry enforced, and it's possible that some recent changes to the pattern of collocation nodes don't work correctly when symmetry is not enforced. So one possible reason for the asymmetry you're seeing is that the full concentric grids are not up/down symmetric: 
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/22567458/120417450-d685c380-c32c-11eb-9bf7-56fd3f831e54.png)
When symmetry is explicitly enforced, we only use the nodes from the top half (0<theta<pi) but for nonsymmetric cases we use the full grid.

Not sure if this is "wrong" per say, as generally if the solution is symmetric it should be imposed explicitly, though I could see an argument that the grid used for non-symmetric cases should still be symmetric. Not sure the best way to do that though, the concentric grids are a bit tricky.

@ddudt thoughts?

I agree the grid is a likely source of this problem.  The concentric grid used to be up/down symmetric, with some nodes at theta=0.  However, when stellarator symmetry is enforced, that grid resulted in some of the force balance equations being linearly dependent.  To avoid that issue we introduced a phase shift in the theta coordinate, giving the grid pictured above which is not up/down symmetric.  

If I remember correctly, this change to the grid was made after the original example in the documentation.  That would help explain why the latest version of the code no longer reproduces that example exactly.  

The linear independence of the force balance equations is only an issue with stellarator symmetry (in general the force error should not have any symmetric structure).  Therefore the "full" (non-symmetric) concentric grid does not need the phase shift in the theta coordinates.  @f0uriest we should probably only add the phase shift for symmetric grids.

OK, making that change seems to help somewhat but doesn't eliminate the asymmetry entirely. I think another possible source is the SVD of the jacobian that's done in the newton method. If the true solution is symmetric but not enforced, and the grid is symmetric, then half the equations will be linearly dependent, so they get removed by the truncated SVD. However, which ones get removed is non-deterministic, and would likely vary each iteration, so there's no guarantee that it will always use the top half or bottom half or some mix of linearly independent equations, so effectively its using a non-symmetric grid.

Closing this for now, because I think the "correct" solution is just to explicitly enforce symmetry when its desired, but feel free to reopen if its still an issue

There's no strong reason. Basically, for the `compute_theta_coords` we know the analytic derivative, while for the vmec one i didn't want to bother deriving it. The main thing is that the jacobian is diagonal because the equations are all decoupled. If we write our own newton method we can take advantage of that to avoid huge matrix operations. The scipy routines all assume a dense jacobian which is both wasteful, and potentially could cause memory issues if you're doing it for like 20k points (except for the diagbroyden method i used in the vmec one, but that only uses an approximate jacobian)

I was able to fix this. In the original version, in __ main __.py, `eq_fam[0]` is created from `VMECIO.load` which created an equilibrium object with L_grid = L etc. When `eq_fam[0] = ir.inputs[0]` is done, it changes the `eq_fam[0].inputs` but not `eq_fam[0].L_grid` etc. We need the equilibrium object `eq_fam[0]` to have attributes as per the input file.
I think a much better way to read equilibrium would be to read the VMEC output into a temporary equilibrium `eq_from_vmec` and then assign only its solution data to `eq_fam[0]`:
```
    if ir.args.vmec is not None:
        # copy equilibrium from vmec output
        eq_from_vmec = VMECIO.load(
            ir.args.vmec,
            L=ir.inputs[0]["L"],
            M=ir.inputs[0]["M"],
            N=ir.inputs[0]["N"],
            spectral_indexing=ir.inputs[0]["spectral_indexing"],
        )
        # assign only the solution data to equil_fam[0]
        equil_fam[0].R_lmn = eq_from_vmec.R_lmn
        equil_fam[0].Z_lmn = eq_from_vmec.Z_lmn
        equil_fam[0].L_lmn = eq_from_vmec.L_lmn
        equil_fam[0].x0 = eq_from_vmec.x0
        equil_fam[0].x = eq_from_vmec.x
```
I used this and it seems to have resolved the issue.

It seems that this happens when continuation is used for pressure_ratio but not when continuation is used for L, M, N. I verified this using the dshape example as well.

When a solution is saved using VMECIO.save and then it's read using VMECIO.load(), it seems to have large force imbalance errors. This may be crucial for using VMEC solutions (.nc) as initial guesses.
Since starting every run from scratch is time-consuming for non-axisymmetric cases, I tried saving an already obtained DESC solution as an .nc file and then using it as a guess using the --vmec flag. But it seems that the bug in VMECIO prevents DESC from using the guess effectively.
I am currently working on using the desc .h5 file itself as a guess which should make resuming/restarting/using a guess easier.
To reproduce an example (files attached):
[DSHAPE_vmecio_bug.zip](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/files/6811918/DSHAPE_vmecio_bug.zip)

`desc DSHAPE`: solve an equilibrium
In python terminal:
`eq1=EquilibriaFamily.load(load_from='DSHAPE_output.h5')[-1]`: load the solution
`plot_section(eq1,"|F|", norm_F=True, log=True)`: check the actual error

`VMECIO.save(eq1,'DSHAPE_output.nc')`: save as .nc
`eq2=VMECIO.load('DSHAPE_output.nc')`: load from the saved .nc
`VMECIO.plot_vmec_comparison(eq1, 'DSHAPE_output.nc')`,`VMECIO.plot_vmec_comparison(eq2, 'DSHAPE_output.nc')`: check if the surfaces match

`plot_section(eq2,"|F|", norm_F=True, log=True)`: check the error for the solution loaded from .nc
![2err](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/84903460/125523020-d4f2bce6-e94d-449f-9634-7e2158916649.png)

Reason 2 that Rory gave is the main issue.  Converting a DESC solution into the VMEC format is exact* because of our spectral basis, but fitting a VMEC solution into that basis introduces numerical errors.  There isn't much we can do to improve the fit because the VMEC solutions are always given on surfaces linearly spaced in toroidal flux, and those quadrature points result in a poorly conditioned system.  The `VMECIO` class was primarily intended to allow DESC equilibria to be used with external codes that expect a VMEC input.  Loading VMEC solutions should be used with caution.  

*The conversion is exact only for R, Z, and lambda. The coefficients of other "derived" quantities such as the magnetic field components must be Fourier transformed from the "real space" data on each surface.  This transform is done with a higher resolution than the primary quantities and seems to be very accurate.

The former only sets it to zero if the attribute doesn't exist. IE, if `_attribute` has a value, it returns that value, otherwise it creates `_attribute` with a value of 0 and returns that. Basically just a guard against weird cases where `_attribute` didn't get created in init or something

For reference, the issue is due to the way JAX compiles things and the way we (try to) reuse those compiled functions where possible. JAX compiles functions based on a fixed shape and datatype of all the input arrays, which basically means that whenever the resolution changes in the multigrid scheme we have to create a new objective function for the new resolution. Recomputing all the transforms and recompiling the function is slow so we try to only do it when really necessary, but the test we had to see if its required wasn't as reliable as needed, so sometimes it would try to use the wrong compiled function. The new version gets rid of this by always rebuilding at every multigrid step just to be safe, at the expense of a slight performance decrease (for now).

^ The compute functions themselves do not know anything about the optimization constraints. If we assign both attributes, then we would need to add a third argument determining which profile to use.

Notes on current input conventions: 
- The input file presently requires giving `d current(rho) / d s`, where `s = rho^2` is the VMEC radial coordinate. So the profile corresponds to the derivative wrt `s`, but it is input in terms of `rho`. This should be an even polynomial in order for the integrated current profile to be an even function. 
- The Equilibrium argument `current_r` expects the profile `d current(rho) / d rho`. This should be an odd polynomial. 
- The Equilibrium argument `current` expects the profile `current(rho)`. This should be an even polynomial. 

While this provides a lot of flexibility for the user to input the current profile in different ways, it could also be confusing (it has already confused me in testing). The logic in the `InputReader` handles the integration wrt `s = rho^2` and passes the `current` argument to the `Equilibrium` class, so the `current_r` argument is unused in typical cases. I propose the following: 
- Remove the `current_r` input from the Configuration/Equilibrium class. 
- Require the user to supply `current(rho)` as the input profile, including in the text-based input file. We can warn them if they give an odd profile or one with nonzero current at the axis. 
- The VMEC-to-DESC input file conversion would still be available for anyone who has profile coefficients in the VMEC format. 

The integration/differentiation wrt rho/psi is trivial for us to perform, but it would also be "trivial" for the user to do it themselves. I think a consistent usage of only `current(rho)` would simplify the code and avoid confusion.

I'm not a fan of mixing flux surface labels in the current input. I understand that VMEC's `s` effectively functions as our `psi` here, but I don't want to know anything about VMEC to run DESC. Also, requiring an input option that is the derivative of a function of one radial coordinate wrt another is weird.

For the `current(rho)` vs `dcurrent(rho) / drho` debate, I _would prefer_ to just allow `current(rho)` as you suggest.

However, I thought we wanted to include the option to give `dcurrent(rho) / drho` because it's theoretically less noisy to integrate than differentiate. If people are generating their input by fitting something, DESC would get more accurate input data if users fit the derivative of their data and give that profile to DESC. If DESC only allows the option to give `current(rho)`, then I doubt anyone will fit their data to a derivative. Do we still think the added noise is an issue?

I'm also not a fan of mixing surface labels. I'd support always converting vmec input into current(rho), and having that be the standard for the desc input file as well. Not sure about keeping the current_r as an option. I can see kaya's point but also I agree it might be unecessary

> I'm also not a fan of mixing surface labels. I'd support always converting vmec input into current(rho), and having that be the standard for the desc input file as well. Not sure about keeping the current_r as an option. I can see kaya's point but also I agree it might be unecessary

One of the reasons the notebook tests are failing because they don't define iota when creating an equilibrium. The master branch relies on [iota defaulting to a power series of 0](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/blob/b154c0d36babf875656a6b428e18491d99e03d0b/desc/configuration.py#L321). On this branch we [set all profiles to None](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/blob/3e6e3df421c5828b402c7c19f53d4599a2aa6dff/desc/configuration.py#L311), and default to vacuum case of [0 current, leaving iota as None](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/blob/3e6e3df421c5828b402c7c19f53d4599a2aa6dff/desc/configuration.py#L337). This [trips](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/blob/3e6e3df421c5828b402c7c19f53d4599a2aa6dff/desc/objectives/linear_objectives.py#L742) the `FixIota.build` method.

The solution is to set `iota = PowerSeriesProfile(0, 0)` in the notebooks.
We should add a guard statement  [here](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/blob/3e6e3df421c5828b402c7c19f53d4599a2aa6dff/desc/objectives/linear_objectives.py#L649) that throws an error `if eq.iota is None`. Users shouldn't fix iota when they haven't specified it.

I've pushed a commit that resolves the original issue Rory raised opened. There is still a discrepancy when `endpoint = True`. More on that at the bottom.


I'm not certain why, but we changed the linear grid spacing computations from `sup = 2pi or 1`, `dx = sup / (max(1, x.size))` to the for loop version of this:
```
if x.size > 1:
    dx[0] = (x[0] + x[1]) / 2
    dx[1:-1] = (x[2:] - x[:-2]) / 2
    dx[-1] = sup - (x[-2] + x[-1]) / 2
else:
    dx = sup
```

Couple separate issues with the above algorithm:
-  `dx[0]` and `dx[-1]` are not computed correctly.  Changing the following fixes that.
    - `dx[0] = x[1] - x[0]`
    - `dx[-1] = sup - x[-1]` 
- it does not compute dzeta correctly. While the zeta nodes depend on NFP, the zeta spacing should not. Fixed by just scaling dz by NFP.

The middle `dx[1:-1]` computation is fine. I'm not sure why it was written that way, as opposed to `dx[0:-1] = np.diff(x)`. Maybe to try and ensure sum(dx) is 2pi.


For the endpoint issue:
Adding an endpoint at 2pi will make `dx[-1] = 2pi - x[-1] = 0` when you pass an array. When you pass an integer, it's not zero (see Dario's screen shot).
Since the point of `endpoint=True` is to duplicate the `theta=0` node at `theta=2pi`, do we want their spacing to be the same?
My thinking is, for theta integral = `sum(dt * something)` then the node at theta=0 should contribute the same weight as the node at theta=2pi.

I feel like true "vacuum" is minimize J with iota free, as J=0 is vacuum, but most people in the community think of minimizing energy (or force) subject to I=0 current constraint as "vacuum"

Those results look pretty different though, and the iota near axis being off is not good either.

the zeta spacing should depend on NFP, since the nodes only go between 0 and 2pi/NFP. I think all you'd need to do is set `sup=2pi/NFP` for zeta. Including an endpoint still does seem to be an issue, I'm not sure of the best fix. In some way it doesn't really make sense since you then have 2 nodes at the same point, assuming you're always doing `linspace(0,sup,n)`. Having `endpoint=True` only really makes sense if you're not going all the way out to `sup`. 
One counterpoint though is that in some of the plotting routines we probably need `endpoint=True` to get stuff to properly close on themselves or plot all the way to the edge of the axis. However, for plotting we don't care about `spacing` or `weights` so it's probably ok if they're "wrong" in that case.

> the zeta spacing should depend on NFP

I think @ddudt and I decided that the spacing shouldn't correspond to the coordinate of a node. Instead it should correspond to the weight of a node. For example, we want `Y = sum(dzeta * some_array)` to not be dependent on NFP. If `dzeta` depends on NFP, then a surface average, which uses integrals like these, would give different results for NFP = 1 and NFP = 2.

(~~An alternative is to always do `Y = sum(dzeta / NFP * some_array)`~~ actually I remember that only works for grids on a single surface grid. I had latex'd something describing that a couple months ago if you want to see)

The zeta and theta spacing inconsistency is fixed. For one thing this means surface averages should now be correct when arrays are past into linear grids.

If there's a duplicate node in the array though, `_scale_weights` doesn't do it's job correctly (here and on `master`). It scales the total volume weight of the node. In general, if there is a theta node repeated N times, we need to just divide the theta spacing of each of those nodes by N, without modifying the rho or zeta spacing. This will make that repeated node contribute the same theta weight as a non-repeated theta node. The current method with `_scale_weights` modifies the rho and zeta spacing when there is a repeated theta node which can cause drho > 1 and dzeta > 2pi.

All the unit tests passed locally. If the regression tests (excluding codecov) pass, we technically could merge this if we needed it now. It fixes the original issue - wrong zeta and theta spacing when constructing a linear grid with an array.

I reverted the changes for the rho spacing back to what they are on `master`. This means passing an array to make a linear grid may still give different rho spacing when `nrho != 1 `. I think the array spacing is actually more correct.

This notebook will be helpful to see the different spacing computed by the old / new methods.
[grid_spacing.zip](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/files/9681348/grid_spacing.zip)

If constraining `I = 0` seems to always be better than minimizing `J = 0` with varying iota, do we still want to support the latter case? It was originally a hack to allow for vacuum solves before we finished implementing the current constraint. 

We could still keep `objective = vacuum` as an input option for minimizing current density instead of force balance, but could do it subject to `I = 0` instead of varying iota.

Yeah with this PR, using `objective=vacuum` and giving no profiles will default to `I=0`, you can still force it to do the free iota version by including iota profile coefficients (which won't be fixed, just used as an initial guess). The differences are small, so its possible in some cases doing free iota might be better (or faster) so I don't think it hurts to leave it as an option.

Inside of the [`isalmostequal`](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/blob/362f6b5be5321b7d4ca41035d3f59dd03449cdee/desc/utils.py#L297) function, the multiplication by the number of elements in the array that is being taken the std of (`*x.shape[axis]` in the line`np.all(x.std(axis=axis) * x.shape[axis] < tol)`) is what takes an array that otherwise has a std of like 1e-14 and pushes it past the 1e-12 tol.

Is this multiplication necessary?

Issue is actually due to numpy.std having numerical precision issues, a solution could be do cast to float128 when doing the np.std call, like 
```
np.all(x.std(axis=axis,dtype=np.float128) * x.shape[axis] < tol)
```

Comment on the math that lets us do this transformation as we forgot one time and it was embarrassing to remember it:

VMEC double angle convention is like :
$A cos(m\theta - n\zeta) + B cos(m\theta + n\zeta)$

Using Ptolemy identity:  
$A cos(m\theta) cos(n\zeta) + A sin(m\theta)sin(n\zeta) + B cos(m\theta)cos(n\zeta) - B sin(m\theta)sin(n\zeta)$

Collect like terms:  
$(A+B) cos(m\theta) cos(n\zeta)  + (A - B) sin(m\theta)sin(n\zeta)$

DESC's convention is double-term like the above lines, so the corresponding DESC coefficients $C,D$ are:
$C cos(m\theta) cos(n\zeta)  + D sin(m\theta)sin(n\zeta) =(A+B) cos(m\theta) cos(n\zeta)  + (A - B) sin(m\theta)sin(n\zeta)$

yielding
$C = A+B$
$D = A - B$

Then rearranging for what the VMEC coefficients a,b are in terms of the DESC coefficients yields
$A = (C+D)/2$
$B = (C-D)/2$

leaving a comment/clarification for my sake, this PR specifically implements inquality constraints for any objective by using a quadratic penalty term that has a dead-zone defined by the bounds passed into the objective (so cost is 0 inside these bounds and is ~ (x-x_bound)^2 where x_bound is the upper or lower bound depending on x > x_upper_bound or x<x_lower_bound)

So any desired inequality constraint MUST be passed in as an OBJECTIVE to the optimization problem, not as a constraint (since constraints are almost always assumed to be linear and then treated by optimizing in the nullspace of that constraint, which does not work for linear inequalities)

> Can any of the plots generated in these new tests be turned into more general plotting routines for `desc/plotting.py`?

I think the new `mpl_image_compare` figures are either pretty specific to testing, so not very likely that users would make variations of them, or basically already covered by the existing `plot_1d()` function. The figures from `test_Redl_figures_2_3`, `test_Redl_figures_4_5`, `test_Redl_sfincs_QA`, and `test_Redl_sfincs_QH` are all for verifying that figures from publications can be reproduced. For plotting `trapped fraction` or `<J*B> Redl` as in `test_trapped_fraction_Kim`, `test_Redl_sfincs_QA`, or `test_Redl_sfincs_QH`, a user could use `plot_1d()` (and SFINCS data as in the latter 2 plots would not be available.) One new plot routine we could contemplate would be a figure with radial profiles of `<J*B>` and `<J*B> Redl` on the same axis, to check self-consistency of the current profile, though that too is perhaps sufficiently covered already by `plot_1d()`.

> A few other general questions:
> 
> * QSC uses Boozer coordinates. When applying the NAE constraints, we convert the Boozer toroidal angle into our standard toroidal angle, but we still use Boozer theta. Is this necessary? Could we write the constraints to use a general theta?

I believe it is necessary for the O(rho) constraints. The way these constraints were derived was converting the X(rho,theta*,phi), Y(rho,theta*,phi) NAE flux surface positions into R(rho,theta*,phi), Z(rho,theta*,phi). These functions in the NAE formalism have the form (at constant phi) of
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/37969854/224138077-cc5a0f22-9c2f-403c-a61f-a729d824e833.png)

we then match that to the form of a function in the plane in Zernike:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/37969854/224138208-b4af0282-95d5-4630-97d6-8ce433719d8e.png)

getting the constraint eqns:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/37969854/224138290-73e9b491-a30f-4910-a56e-84177183165d.png)

this is only possible since we assumed the poloidal angle is the same for each of these functional forms. If the Zernike one was generalized, we would have to replace $\theta$ everywhere by $\theta_{DESC} + \lambda(\rho,\theta_{DESC},\phi)$ and the simple relation between the NAE coefficients and the Zernike coefficients is lost (we can't simple just match terms on either side anymore, and I am not sure of how we would deal with all of the cos($\lambda$) terms which are each functions of $(\rho,\theta_{DESC}.\phi$) 

> * The API for getting NAE constraints is a bit different from the others, in that we need to pass in the QSC and eq objects to the utility function. Would it be possible to put the logic from `nae_utils` into the build method of a specialized class?

Do you mean like an objective class `NearAxisConstraint` that just internally creates the necessary constraints and takes as argument a qsc, but not necessarily an equilibrum, and the NAE constraints that are in the nae_utils.py would be created when this overarching constraint is built? I suppose I see how that could be useful/more intuitive than having this helper function

> * Also, I assume all this stuff also works for QIC? can we add a test to make sure?

I have not tested but can add a test

> * In the examples/notebook, the NAE constraints are always applied to an equilibrium that was first created by doing `Equilibrium.from_near_axis`. Is this necessary? Or could you just create some arbitrary equilibrium and then apply the NAE behavior from a QSC equilibrium?

This is not actually something I've tried, I can test it. But, currently the util function for NAE constraints assumes that the axis you want fixed is the equilibrium's current axis, which I assume is the qsc axis. It does not make much sense to fix O(r) behavior with a different axis. I should change the function so it always tries to fix the QSC axis, that is an oversight on my part.

Right but sometimes the default grid wasn't used, which can then make it misleading when the equilibrium is loaded, and the solution is not the solution from the default grid. This happens when I run higher-resolution equilibria, where the default grid would be pretty large, so I use a smaller grid.

Also, the default grid when you create an equilibrium is 1.5* LMN (for ANSI), but from an input file if you don't specify grid resolutions the [default grid is 2*LMN ](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/blob/5edf6b419b08c49144dd213f1cb202f86765b4b7/desc/io/input_reader.py#L597), so this can cause an additional source of mismatch when you load in an equilibrium solved from an input file

I agree, we should fix this. Right now they're used somewhat interchangeably in many places, but they shouldn't be. In all of the optimizers that we have so far, one iteration means one accepted step by the optimizer, which may need more than 1 function evaluation. Generally each iteration requires one evaluation and factorization of the jacobian/hessian, which is the primary cost of the optimization, so iterations also correspond more closely to time. To me it makes sense to have the primary thing be `maxiter`, but right now the input file only has `nfev` so thats the main place we'd need to change it, but not sure the best way. Do we want to allow both? Or throw deprecation warnings etc?

with the parameter $\alpha=1$, the softmax is always greater than the actual max bc $log(\sum_i^N e^x_i) > log(e^x_{max})$. Then because we find the softmin by taking `-softmax(-arr)`, the softmin is also always going to be less than the actual min. So this should provide a conservative estimate of these values, which is the way we would like to lean for this type of calculation (i.e. if our bound is we want a minimum distance from the vessel, using softmin should get us at least that distance away,  if not more, since it is a conservative estimate of the minimum that is lower than the real minimum)

I think I understand now. Let's say h(r, t, z) is the volume Jacobian. Currently if the broadcast `(data["sqrt(g)"] * q.T).T` succeeds, then so will `(data["sqrt(g)"] * surface_integrals(q).T).T`, for any dimension of `q` from 0 to 3.

As you mention, when the input `q` has 2 dimensions, we typically expect a square array for `q` because `f` and `g` as defined in my comments for the surface integral function will typically both have size `grid.num_nodes`. Because it is a square matrix, we need to be careful about broadcasting; wherever a broadcast succeeds with `q` it will also succeed with `q.T`. Yet only one of those operations can be our intention. The same applies to the algorithm in `surface_integrals`; we should make sure we are doing the integration along the correct axis, and that you and I do not have our axes swapped.

The way I visualize what this PR does is as follows.

- As always when the quantity to integrate `q` has shape `(grid.num_nodes, )` for example `q=data["sqrt(g)"]`, I think of it as a function over the nodes in some space like R^3. Each node is mapped to a number and `surface_integrals(q)` will sum, over a particular surface, all of those numbers. It does this for each surface. The output will again be a function in R^3, but now each surface is mapped to a number, which is of course constant over the surface.
- This PR generalizes the integration routine to work for a more complicated integrand, that is when the dimension of the integrand `q` increases. When `q` has shape `(grid.num_nodes, f_size)`, now each node is mapped to `f_size` amount of numbers which represents some function discretized at `f_size` points. `surface_integrals(q)` will sum, over a particular surface, all of those functions. It does this for each surface. The output maps each surface to a summed function. If there are 10 surfaces on the grid, then, semantically, this approach performs 10 surface integrals, so the output will be ten such unique summed functions. (Before expanding, `surface_integrals(q).shape == (10, f_size)`.).

Or did you have a different algorithm for integrating a 2d quantity such as:
Still map each node to some `f` but instead perform `surface_integrals(f)` for every node. Then your output will map each node to a function which is potentially different from other nodes' on a particular surface in the computational domain (rho, theta, zeta). With this intention, you should not `expand` the output because you already have your `grid.num_nodes` amount of unique quantities which is going to be broadcastable with quantities like `data["sqrt(g)"]`.

Although these two algorithms are different, their implementations only differ by a transpose.
Edit: this transpose is already done by the user though. So the only difference is that the former algorithm should be expanded to be consistent while the latter should not.

If your use case is the latter, we should make that a new function because it's different. The former is more consistent with `surface_integrals` in the one dimensional case.

Putting aside the limits, if the question was wondering what we should do in general for the derivatives, then I think anytime we take derivatives in the code it should be the derivative of the vector itself. Going back to that slack message with the transformation between coordinate systems, it makes sense to me that you should differentiate $B$ with respect to $z$ after transforming it to the computational coordinates. This is because the linear transform, $T$, itself depends on $z$, so $dB(\rho, \theta, \zeta)/dz = d (T(B(x, y, z)))/dz = (dT/dz) B(x, y, z) + T dB(x, y, z)/dz$, where the derivative $dT/dz$ is the component wise matrix derivative of $T$.

In that sense the vector $dB/dz$ should not be independent of the coordinate system. This is because the linear operator that is the derivative with respect to $z$, denoted $D_z$, does not commute with the linear transformation $T(z)$, intuitively because the output of $T$ depends on $z$.

Are we sure that the test isn't just set up to do finite differencing on the components of the vectors, instead of doing finite differencing on the vector itself? We want
$$ \delta A( \rho, \theta, \zeta ) = A( \rho + \delta \rho, \theta, \zeta ) - A( \rho, \theta, \zeta ) $$
which should also subtract the basis vectors from one another.

> Are we sure that the test isn't just set up to do finite differencing on the components of the vectors, instead of doing finite differencing on the vector itself. We want $\delta A(\rho, \theta, \zeta) = A(\rho + \delta \rho, \theta, \zeta) - A(\rho, \theta, \zeta) $ which should also subtract the basis vectors from one another.

Doing it like that does correctly difference the basis vectors `e_rho`, `e_theta`, `e_zeta`, however, those vectors themselves are expressed in cylindrical coordinates, which depend on the angle `phi`. So its effectively only differentiating the components of the vector in the cylindrical basis, `[dB_R/d*, dB_phi/d*, dB_Z/d*]`. What we actually want is the derivative of the vector `B_R*Rhat + B_phi*phihat + B_Z*Zhat`, and the easiest way to do that is to convert it to cartesian where the derivative of the basis vectors is zero, then we can differentiate the components as usual.

The vector itself is physical and shouldn't depend on the coordinate system, but the triplet of numbers we use to represent the vector does depend on the basis, hence having to convert to a standard basis before differentiating.

If you know a priori that the limit of some vector exists then, in an orthogonal coordinate system, this implies the limit of each component exists ${}^1$. If the limit of each component exists and each component has the $0/0$ form (meaning you know those limits in the numerator and denominator exist too; this is the extra condition you need since the limits are multivariable), then you can use the proof I gave to show the limit of the vector is the vector of quotients of partial derivatives. Also what makes a quantity physical? I see why we can't have infinite B field, but derivatives of physical quantities are less intuitive. Volume seems physical, yet if I parameterize it by $V(x) = x^{1/2}$ for some variable $x$, then the derivative of volume is not bounded at $x=0$.

The footnote below answers whether the derivative of the vector itself or the component-wise derivative should be taken to evaluate the limit.

${}^1$ In a non-orthogonal system, the latter condition is stricter than the former because the components may be unbounded in isolation yet still cancel in combination. To see this algebraically, notice that the limit we want to compute is the leftmost quantity given below. Each relation following only holds if more assumptions are made. My approach in this PR of computing the limits computes the second from rightmost quantity. Computing the limits of vectors via differentiating the components is computing the rightmost quantity. That quantity is technically less likely to exist and would require adding more dependencies to compute (and if it exists is guaranteed to equal the quantity to its left).

$$\lim \frac{X}{Y} \equiv \lim \left( \frac{x_1}{y_1} e_1 + \frac{x_2}{y_2} e_2 + \frac{x_3}{y_3} e_3 \right) = \lim \left( \frac{x_1}{y_1} e_1 \right) + \lim \left( \frac{x_2}{y_2} e_2 \right) + \lim \left( \frac{x_3}{y_3} e_3 \right) = \lim \left( \frac{x_1}{y_1} \right) \lim e_1 + \lim \left( \frac{x_2}{y_2} \right) \lim e_2 + \lim \left( \frac{x_3}{y_3} \right)  \lim e_3$$

Are we sure we want to do this integral along its boundary? Using this technique to compute $V(\rho)$ was a good idea because
1. The integration becomes more tractable. We only need to consider n^2 rather than n^3 points, so this also leads to higher accuracy
2. Transforming the integration to one over periodic domains makes it more accurate, especially at low resolution, (midpoint rule integral on periodic domains converge exponentially to true integral).
3. We knew a cheap to compute transformation with $\nabla \cdot Z = 1$.

For $B(\rho)$, point 2 is still valid, but maybe less important as I'd expect an integral over less dimensions to have less issues with accuracy. ~~For point 1 -- if we still want to take the mean of the cross sectional area over all $\zeta$ surfaces, then while integrating along the boundary reduces the dimension of each integral it doesn't reduce the number of integrals that need to be done. Instead of finding a vector potential it's easier to integrate along the boundary like:

$\iint_D dS (\nabla \cdot A) = \int_{\partial D} d\ell (n \cdot A)$ where $n$ is the normal vector to the coordinate curve. Since we want $d \ell$ to parametrize the boundary of a $\rho$ surface at constant $\zeta$, the tangent vector to the curve points in direction $e_{\theta}$, so the normal vector points in direction $n = \partial_{\theta} e_{\theta}$.

```python
def other_way_to_compute_area(eq, grid):
    data = eq.compute(["g_tt", "Z", "e_theta_t", "rho"], grid=grid)
    # line length Jacobian, dl or tangent vector magnitude
    dl = np.sqrt(data["g_tt"])
    # unit normal vector to coordinate curve
    n = -(data["e_theta_t"].T / np.linalg.norm(data["e_theta_t"], axis=-1)).T
    # 2d cylindrical divergence (fix zeta) of Z over zeta surface is 1
    q = dl * n[:, 2] * data["Z"]  # Z is the A in divergence theorem in github comment above

    # In theory this part can be made into just 1 integral with some changes to line_integrals function
    A = np.empty(grid.num_rho)  # this is the cross-sectional area A(r) as function of rho
    for i, r in enumerate(grid.compress(data["rho"])):
        A[i] = np.mean(
            line_integrals(
                grid=grid,
                q=q,
                line_label="theta",
                fix_surface=("rho", r),
                expand_out=False,
            )
        )
    # axis limit is 0
    return A
```

Caoxiang also showed that using the actual tangents to the curve instead of the linear piecewise linear approximation also helps a lot, and would work for splines as well since it only requires first derivatives (offsetting the points is based on the local curvature which is higher order)

@ddudt @f0uriest I figured out why the original line integral failed for ellipses. The original code I provided assumes the curve is parameterized with unit speed (e.g. in the Fenet Frame or parameterized by arc length). For eliptical cross sections, a curve parameterized by $\theta$ does not travel at unit speed.

For a parameterization with non-constant speed, the unit normal vector cannot be computed as the derivative of the tangent vector of the curve (i.e. the acceleration) because some component of the acceleration vector must point along the tangent curve to change the speed of parameterization. In general for curves with arbitrary parameterizations, we can compute the unit normal vector as the acceleration vector minus the component of the acceleration vector along the tangent vector.

The integration along the boundary is provided below is correct and avoids the numerical errors that come with a trapezoidal integration. If `V(r) / (2*pi*R0)` always works then yea that is probably nicer.

```python
def area_boundary_line_integral(eq, grid):
    data = eq.compute(["g_tt", "Z", "e_theta", "e_theta_t", "rho"], grid=grid)
    # line length Jacobian (tangent vector magnitude)
    dl = np.sqrt(data["g_tt"])
    # unit tangent vector
    tangent = (data["e_theta"].T / dl).T
    # outward unit normal vector
    normal = -(data["e_theta_t"].T - dot(data["e_theta_t"], tangent) * tangent.T).T
    normal = (normal.T / np.linalg.norm(normal, axis=-1)).T
    # 2d cylindrical divergence (fix zeta) of Z over zeta surface is 1
    integrand = dl * normal[:, 2] * data["Z"]

    # with some changes to line_integrals function this for loop can be removed
    A = np.array(
        [
            line_integrals(
                grid,
                integrand,
                line_label="theta",
                fix_surface=("rho", r),
                expand_out=False,
            ).mean()
            for r in grid.compress(data["rho"])
        ]
    )
    # axis limit is 0
    return A
```

I prefer names like `iota_from_current` and `iota_in_vacuum` by the way.

To compute `iota_from_current` and its derivatives, you should be able to just copy the compute functions for `iota` and replace all references to `iota_num` with the term `alpha` defined in the compute functions for `iota_num`. (similar with `iota_num_r` and `alpha_r`). This will also give you the correct limits.

Same thing for `iota_in_vacuum` except use the term `beta` instead.


Currently on master, the only physics constraint I used to compute these limits is that the magnetic field is physical. (This was necessary because there is an if and only if relationship between this and the limit of iota being finite).

FYI, there are two other perhaps weaker physics conditions which can make computing the limits easier. These conditions are that $\partial_{\rho} \iota$ and $\partial_{\rho} I$ are both zero at axis. I didn't explicitly enforce these and computed the limits in the more general manner because

2. didn't want to assume behavior of user-inputted quantities

The new quantities are working except for the axis limit of iota from the current. I think I understand why: 

I changed the references from things like `2 * jnp.pi * mu_0 * profiles["current"].compute(params["c_l"], dr=0)` to instead be like `4 * jnp.pi**2 * data["I"]`. This moves away from depending on the current profile as an input, so that we could compute these new quantities even when the user gives an iota profile instead. This also better matches Kaya's equations. 

The axis limits then depend on the value of `data["I_rr"]` instead of `profiles["current"].compute(params["c_l"], dr=2)`. The later is always well defined at the axis by the input, but the former is computed as a flux surface average of $B_\theta$. It appears that in our code this always evaluates to `I_rr = 0` at the axis, even though it should generally have a finite value. So we need to implement the proper axis limit for that quantity to finish this work.

For iota and current, we can specify the profiles as an array of polynomial coefficients. Can't we do the same for the pressure profile without this commit?

> For iota and current, we can specify the profiles as an array of polynomial coefficients. Can't we do the same for the pressure profile without this commit?

There's 2 aspects to this. Any profile is represented as a `Profile` object, which can indeed be a power series, spline, etc. This determines what the degrees of freedom are for the given profile. This PR doesn't change any of that. What it changes is how we target a particular profile during optimization. Usually we just fix all the profiles, using something like `FixPressure`, `FixIota` etc. This fixes the degrees of freedom of the profile, whether they be polynomial coefficients or values of the profile at spline knots. 

However, if we're not fixing the profile, because we want to match it only approximately, or we want to have it between some bounds (eg, iota should be "near" 0.42 or core pressure should be between 10 and 12 kpa) then the `Fix*` constraints won't really work. That's what the profile objectives like `RotationalTransform`, `ToroidalCurrent`, and the new `Pressure` objective are for. They allow you to target or bound the values of the profile as a function of rho without worrying about the underlying representation (power series or spline or whatever). For example, if I want my pressure to lie between two bounds, we would usually think of those bounds as functions of rho. Translating those bounds into constraints on polynomial coefficients is generally pretty tricky, so it's easier to just specify the bounds or target as a function of rho, which this PR allows.

This is likely poor notation on our part.

Our "regular" `sqrt(g)` is the determinate of the coordinate transform between DESC coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \zeta)$ and the lab frame $(R, \phi, Z)$, and same for `sqrt(g)_PEST` = $(\rho, \theta_{PEST}, \zeta) -> (R, \phi, Z)$

However, what we call `sqrt(g)_B` is really the determinate of the coordinate change between boozer coordinates and DESC coordinates (not the lab frame): `sqrt(g)_B` = $(\rho, \theta, \zeta) -> (\rho, \theta_B, \zeta_B)$

The actual equation is $$\sqrt{g}_B = (1 + \partial \lambda /\partial \theta) * (1 + \partial \nu / \partial \zeta ) + (\iota - \partial \lambda / \partial \zeta) * \partial \nu / \partial \theta$$

Which in axisymmetry reduces down to what you have above but without the factor of $\sqrt{g}$

Yeah, it's definitely larger difference that we should see from just compilation, I think the actual source of the discrepancy is here:

https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/blob/9f31227d3f8fafe11002d2ff603cc15ffcaa6b2c/desc/equilibrium/equilibrium.py#L768

In `eq.compute` we do some extra logic to ensure things are computed on the "correct" grids (ie, make sure we get accurate volume and surface averages for things that require them). This was done to ensure that stuff like computing `iota` at a single point worked correctly. 

To be conservative we generally oversample the grid resolution by ~2 to account for nonlinearity and aliasing. If you change your `QuadratureGrid` to have `M=eq.M_grid`, `N=eq.N_grid` I get the same values using both methods, regardless of any compilation.

The confusion mostly occurs when creating a custom `Grid`, and in that case I think we can just have `sort` default to false. The only reason we sort things is so they're aligned correctly for doing an FFT, but with a custom grid its very unlikely that the other requirements for an fft would be met (ie equal spacing, same rho/theta at each zeta) so it's probably not worth it for that case.

Correction to the pressure scaling from force balance:

$B \sim c_B$

$J = \nabla \times B \sim \frac{B}{R} \sim \frac{c_B}{c_R}$

$\nabla p = J \times B \sim \frac{c_B^2}{c_R}$

$p \sim R \nabla p \sim c_B^2$

So the pressure profile actually has no dependence on the major radius scaling $c_R$.

What is "things" exactly? An object of a class, list, dict ?

This PR is basically about changing how we keep track of and organize all the variables that eventually get passed to the optimizer. Previously, everything we wanted to optimize was an attribute of an `Equilibrium`, and we had a hard-coded list of those attributes: https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/blob/b6ede28b7717ed6bb85789f2e3d558a778e6126c/desc/compute/utils.py#L1279

This list also defined how we order the parameters when we put them all in a single array to pass to the optimizer.

The big limitation of this is it doesn't generalize well to doing stuff like coil optimization, winding surface stuff, omnigenity with target fields etc.

So now we introduce a new base class `Optimizable` that tells the code "Hey, this object is something we might want to optimize, here are its degrees of freedom (decorated with `@optimizable_parameter`) and some methods for getting/setting/stacking/unstacking those parameters"

Each objective is bound to one or more `Optimizable` objects. For most objectives, this is just a single `Equilibrium`, but for example, `PlasmaVesselDistance` connects an `Equilibrium` to a `Surface`. Similarly, future work will add stuff like `QuadraticFlux` for connecting an `Equilibrium` or `Surface` to external coils, or the new omnigenity stuff where we have both an `Equilibrium` and a target `OmnigeneousField`. These different objects are what's stored in `things`. Each sub-objective (ie, force, qs, aspect ratio etc) knows about what things it is connected to, and the overall objective (`ObjectiveFunction`) collects all those things into a unique set. The `things` attribute is generally a collection (list, tuple, or nested list, tuple) of `Optimizable` objects, each of which in turn has specific optimizable parameters like `R_lmn`, `p_l`, etc.

The key point is that there's no longer some single master list of all the possible parameters we might want to optimize. Instead, each `Optimizable` object can declare it's own parameters and their sizes, types, meanings etc, without the rest of the code needing to know about it. When we're optimizing stuff, the `ObjectiveFunction` doesn't need to know all the individual parameters that are used, just which `Optimizable` things are involved. Each thing then is in charge of knowing what it's parameters are and how to convert them into a single array that the optimizer sees.

Renamed the function to `flip_helicity` and it will always be applied when called, so could be used to make profiles negative if they are already positive. 

Also added more tests. The basis vectors $e_\rho$, $e_\theta$, and $e^\zeta$ are unchanged. $R_\zeta$ and $Z_\zeta$ do flip sign, which changes $e_\zeta$, but these components of the vector are not used to compute $\sqrt{g}$. The QH helicity flips its sign.

constrain* spelling error

_ddudt commented on 2023-11-20T20:00:05Z_ ----------------------------------------------------------------

Yes, the extra degree of freedom is the width of the well.

In this example we have three spline knots on the axis (and on every other surface too). We fix two of those values to B_min and B_max to give us the desired mirror ratio, but that third spline knot is still free to vary. It represents the value of |B| at the midpoint (in eta) between B_min and B_max.

Technically this third spline knot is not constrained to stay within the bounds (B_min, B_max). But we initialize it in the middle and it stays well behaved.

@ddudt The computation is working correctly. Here is a jupyter notebook with a visual of what is discussed below [elongation_test.zip](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/files/13866106/elongation_test.zip). There I confirm the results we compute match the analytic result from sympy.

The reason we are getting a wrong value for `a_major/a_minor` in `test_elongation` on symmetric grids is a resolution issue. The two grids
```python
fg = LinearGrid(L=2, M=eq.M_grid, N=2, sym=False, NFP=eq.NFP)
sg = LinearGrid(L=2, M=eq.M_grid, N=2, sym=True, NFP=eq.NFP)
```
place nodes at different locations in $\theta$. To compute the elongation, we compute a perimeter of a constant $\zeta$ surface by integrating $\Vert \mathbf{e}_{\theta} \Vert$  over $\theta$.  For the particular surface used in `test_elongation`, the quadrature estimates the true integral better when we sample the integrand at the nodes used by `fg` than it does when we sample at the nodes used by `sg`. At reasonable resolution, this difference is not measurable because our midpoint scheme integration will converge to the true integral exponentially on the periodic domain over $\theta$. Increasing `eq.M_grid` from 2 to 4 will pass the test.

As a sanity check , after the fixes in #451 , we can construct a symmetric grid that has the same nodes as `fg` like this:
```python
unique_theta = fg.nodes[fg.unique_theta_idx, 1]
sg_manual = LinearGrid(
    L=2, theta=unique_theta[unique_theta <= np.pi], N=2, sym=True, NFP=eq.NFP
)
```
I have checked computations on `sg_manual` match `fg` at all resolutions.


(some details just for your information: The reason `sg` does not have the same node placement at `sg_manual` is just a design choice:
When a number is passed in for `L, M, N` (or rho, theta, zeta) on `LinearGrid`, we want to construct a grid where all the nodes are weighted equally in any integration etc. The simplest way to do this is to use node placement such that `grid.spacing` and `grid.weights` can be the the same across every node (like it is for `fg`).  When symmetry is set to `true`, it is only correct for `grid.spacing` and `grid.weights` to be the same across every node if the nodes are evenly spaced. This requires that the arc distance between the closest node to $\theta = \pi$ and its reflection across the $\theta = \pi$ axis (let's call this its left neighbor assuming counterclock wise is left) equals the distance to the node to its right. In particular, this means there can't be a node at $\theta = 0$ since that distance is 0, so `sg` must have a different node placement than `fg` in order for `sg.spacing` and `sg.weights` to be constant.

When the node placement is explicitly specified, as in `sg_manual`, it seems important to respect that placement and not change anything. For the grid `sg_manual`,  the attributes `sg.spacing` and  `sg.weights` are not constant - in particular, the nodes at $\theta \neq 0$ have double the weight and spacing as the node at $\theta = 0$ because we need to double count the ones at $\theta \neq 0$  since there would have been effectively been two of them in an integration if we had not deleted the nodes with $\theta > \pi$. This ensures that all computations on `sg_manual` match those of `fg`.
)

For example we prioritize correctness of surface integrals over line integrals as mentioned [in the docstring here](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/blob/b5921fd37016ef13999e5f1157d3ad0931602bc3/desc/compute/utils.py#L676). This could be fixed by creating an alias attribute `grid.line_spacing` that returns `grid.spacing` if there are no duplicate nodes or a different array of shape `(grid.num_nodes, 3)` when there are duplicates.

this ordering works. The issue is that when `objective.build` is called, `objective.things` gets set in the order of whatever the first objective in the tuple of objectives given to `ObjectiveFunction` is. Then later on in `optimizer.optimize` line 292 when `objective.unpack_state` is called on the `xi` in `results["allx"]`, the x is unpacked into the order of the `objective.things`, which can possibly differ from the order of `things` passed into `optimizer.optimize`, thus leading to the mismatch when the params are assigned to the final objects in line 308

> I think the better API would be to introduce new degrees of freedom Rp, Zp etc like we have for the LCFS and axis, and then constrain those to be self consistent.
> 
> This would eliminate the `boundary_mode` thing, and allow more flexibility for setting up constraints.
> 
> Each equilibrium, in addition to having a `.surface` and `.axis` attribute would have a `.poincare` or `.section` property with the ZernikeRZToroidalSurface object. This would then have an assigned zeta value so we wouldn't need to pass around zeta to different functions.

@f0uriest I made some changes to the API. First of all, I created a new class called PoincareSurface (which is an inherited class of ZernikeRzToroidalSection) to be able to store lambda basis and coefficients in the section. That class needs more cleaning but my main aim is to decide which type of objectives to use by checking the eq.surface type. This can be either FourierRZToroidalSurface or PoincareSurface. I changed the previous eq.bdry_mode stuff to that. Also, I am using the zeta of the surface now, so no need to pass zeta value to optimizer and objectives anymore.

I'm a bit confused by the use of gauss-chebyshev above. You factor out the $1/\sqrt(1-x^2)$ but the leftover part still has a $1/\sqrt(1-\lambda B)$ which is still singular at the endpoints. Even if you avoid evaluating it at the endpoints, its still a singular integrand which likely won't be well approximated by a polynomial, unless there's something I'm missing?

Yes, the term 1/sqrt(1-lambda B) is singular at the endpoints but by virtue of Gauss-Chebyshev quadrature, none of the quadrature points will lie at the singular points. You can get arbitrarily close without actually being at the singular point.

The objective is not to transform the singularity into some nice, non-singular integral but to use a robust quadrature that excludes the singular points without excluding the contributions of the integrand near the integrable singularities.

The `desc.objectives` won't directly give what you want, as we do not use the boundary modes as arguments to our functions, but rather the coefficients of the basis describing the whole solution (JAX gives derivatives wrt the arguments of the function). What you want, I assume, is the derivative of iota with respect to the boundary modes at constant force error (which one would find with VMEC normally by repeatedly calling the equilibrium solve with slightly different boundary shapes)

DESC can do this with one eq solve (or one jacobian creation for the force balance objective) This is what is internally done in the `perturbations.py` `optimal_perturb` function, which more or less attempts to find a change in the inputs $c$ (this is the boundary coefficients, profiles, and Psi) that will improve the objective $g$ (e.g. iota, QS, etc) while approximately maintaining zero force balance (see [this paper](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-plasma-physics/article/desc-stellarator-code-suite-part-3-quasisymmetry-optimization/0B262B685969D2F5697BEE28C8A78DB1) for more detail)

I think something like this is what you want:

```python
import desc
from desc.objectives import ObjectiveFunction, RotationalTransform, ForceBalance
from desc.optimize import ProximalProjection

eq = desc.examples.get("DSHAPE_CURRENT")

objective = ObjectiveFunction(RotationalTransform(eq, target=1.2, loss_function="mean"))
constraint = ObjectiveFunction(ForceBalance(eq))

prox = ProximalProjection(objective, constraint, eq)
prox.build()

x = prox.x(eq) # vector of all the boundary/profile dofs
jac = prox.jac_scaled(x) # d(iota)/d(boundary + profile dofs)

import jax
# unpack the big matrix into dict of individual components
jax.vmap(prox.unpack_state, (0, None))(jac, False)[0]
```

The `ProximalProjection` thing basically takes care of solving the equilibrium and combining all the jacobians together to give you the derivative you want wrt the boundary terms. However be aware that it maintains state, and so if you evaluate at a different x it will update the equilibrium to that new state. It uses a perturb/re-solve method, so it only really works if you call it with a sequence of xs that aren't changing too quickly (which is fine for gradient based optimization but might cause issues if you're doing global stuff, let me know and we can probably modify it to deal with that)

Here's a detailed comparison of these quadratures for a simple shifted circle case.

![Quad_comparison](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/assets/19224702/f9e28e60-c938-44d2-a135-6f92e8a8567a)

* At lower resolutions Gauss-Chebyshev is more accurate, especially for the integral of the type 1/sqrt(1-lambda B).
* At each resolution, sinh-tanh quadrature takes around 40% longer than Gauss-Chebyshev. Most of the time is spent to calculate the weights and quadrature points so that can just be done once for the whole calculation.
* Sinh-tanh is clearly a better method but I would still like to keep both quadratures since there may be differences when we do this for a more complicated geometry.
* The transformation from [-theta_b, theta_b] -> [-1, 1] can have many different forms, I chose a sin function but you can choose any odd function of the form x^{n} or x^{1/n} where n is an odd number or any invertible function. One can use arcsin if they want.

Closing this for now as it seems like there isn't really a way to make it efficient, it basically ends up about as expensive as the cholesky method, plus the cost of the QR

want to solve

$$
\min_p ||Jp + f||   \quad s.t. ||p|| = \delta
$$

equivalent to 

$$
(J^T J + \alpha I)p = -J^T f
$$

for some $\alpha \geq 0$

writing $J = QR$

$$
(R^TQ^T Q R + \alpha I)p = -R^T Q^T f
$$

$Q$ is orthogonal:

$$
(R^T R + \alpha I)p = -R^T Q^T f
$$

write $I = R^{-1} R$

$$
(R^T R + \alpha R^{-1} R)p = -R^T Q^T f
$$

$$
(R^T + \alpha R^{-1})Rp = -R^T Q^T f
$$

Not really any savings because although $R$ is triangular, $(R^T + \alpha R^{-1})$ doesn't have any particular structure so we're back to regular inversion
